doctrine: Interactive assessment framework to identify competitive advantages when starting a venture. Core methodology: map resources (business access, equipment, IP, reach), experience across 3+ industries (role, timeline, problems solved, rated 1-10 skill + network), network depth by category (industry experts, potential clients, referral sources, advisors, technical specialists), skills self-assessment (project management, data, systems, process improvement, customer discovery, sales/marketing, finance), and interest alignment. Rank advantages strongest-to-weakest (business ownership > deep experience + network > experience alone > network alone > interest alone). Reality-check gates: name specific expensive problems, verify people pay for solutions, confirm access to decision-makers, assess market stability/growth. Decision framework: should you pick a niche now? (Clear advantages / Not yet, explore more / Uncertain, need outside perspective). Anti-patterns: forcing false advantages, chasing trends, entering markets with zero connections, betting on weak advantages, ignoring spending behavior. 8-section workbook: What You Have (access + resources) / What You Know (experience rating + depth) / Who You Know (mapped network) / What You're Good At (skills + interests) / Your Real Advantages (ranked top 3) / Reality Check (4-gate validation per advantage) / Decision and Next Steps / Implementation timeline.
gates: Network mapping by relationship quality and value type
Can you name specific, expensive problems people have
Do you know people actually paying for solutions now
Can you reach the decision-makers directly
workflows: Map 1-5 current business access points and revenue/headcount
Audit 3-4 prior roles: industry, scope, problems solved, skill/network ratings
Inventory 5 network tiers: industry knowledge, potential clients, referral sources, trusted advisors, technical specialists
Rank top 3 genuine advantages and interrogate copyability
Validate each advantage against 4 reality-check gates
Make niche decision: commit / stay broad / get outside perspective
Plan month 1 and quarter testing cadence
prompts: What's your situation? (Own, co-own, have decision power, influence only, no access)
Could you test new ideas there? (business access leverage test)
What did you get really good at? (skill extraction from prior roles)
How well do you know this industry? (1-10)
How connected are you in this space? (1-10)
Why is this actually true? (advantage reality-check)
Why can't others easily copy this? (moat interrogation)
Can you name specific, expensive problems people have? (problem market validation)
Do you know people who are actually paying for solutions now? (customer proof)
Can you actually reach the people who make buying decisions? (sales access)
Is this market growing or at least stable? (market viability)
operating_rules: Be honest about advantages; do not fabricate edges
Experience and network depth matter more than credentials
Decision-maker access trumps general social proof
Existing paying customers beat theoretical demand
Copying barrier (moat) is a critical reality-check
Strong interest without experience/connections ranks last
Unknown niche is preferable to forced niche
Test assumptions before committing to market focus
Revisit assessment quarterly or after major transitions
content_ideas: Case study: how an advantage maps to a specific business win
Assessment remix: advantages for B2B services vs e-commerce vs SaaS
Moat-building playbook: how each advantage type creates defensibility
Network depth vs breadth: when to narrow vs expand relationships
Testing framework: validation checklist for each advantage tier
Industry-specific edge inventory: tech vs healthcare vs real estate
weird_gold: Network relationships scored 1-10 are actionable; generic connection counts are useless.
Market stability matters as much as growth; declining but still paying is better than hot but speculative.
Can-copy-easily is the inverse of moat; most advantages fail this gate.
Decision-maker texting distance is an underrated deal-signal.
Strong interest alone is explicitly ranked LAST; motivation without leverage is low-signal.
notes: This is a structured self-assessment workbook. It contains no novel theory, no proprietary methodology (all elements are standard venture/consulting assessment), and no tactical IP. Value is in the scaffolding: it forces honest inventory and reality-checks rather than gut-feel niche selection. Suitable as a lead-gen assessment or intake workbook (pre-consulting call), but not a standalone doctrine. Best used as a diagnostic tool before building a comprehensive business model or GTM strategy.
